lesson.title: The Neuron's Standby Mode: Understanding Resting Potential
lesson.summary: Resting potential is the stable negative electrical charge, about negative 70 millivolts, that a neuron maintains across its membrane when it is not actively firing, providing the baseline state from which every neural signal begins.
lesson.body:
Even when a neuron is not sending a signal, it is not truly idle. It sits at a resting potential of roughly negative 70 millivolts, meaning the inside of the cell is electrically negative compared to the outside. This is not an "off" state so much as a poised, ready state, similar to a bow held drawn: no arrow has been released yet, but tension is stored and available the instant it is needed.

This voltage difference exists because ions are distributed unevenly across the neuron's membrane. Potassium ions, K+, are far more concentrated inside the cell, while sodium ions, Na+, and chloride ions, Cl-, are far more concentrated outside it. Large negatively charged protein molecules synthesized inside the cell are also trapped there and cannot cross the membrane at all, which adds further to the negative charge sitting inside relative to outside. These four pieces together, K+ high inside, Na+ and Cl- high outside, and trapped anions adding negative charge, set up the raw ingredients for a voltage difference.

The membrane itself is selectively permeable, meaning it does not treat every ion the same. At rest it is considerably leakier to K+ than to Na+, since it has many more open potassium leak channels than sodium leak channels embedded in it. This means K+ tends to drift out of the cell down its concentration gradient faster than Na+ drifts in, and that net outward movement of positive charge is the major reason the cell's interior settles into a negative resting voltage, close to, though not identical to, potassium's own equilibrium point, the voltage at which the outward pull of the concentration gradient exactly balances the inward electrical pull of the negative interior.

Left alone, this arrangement would slowly break down as ions leaked across the membrane and gradients flattened out toward equilibrium. The sodium-potassium pump prevents that slow collapse. Using energy from ATP, it actively transports three Na+ ions out of the cell for every two K+ ions it brings back in, working continuously against both ions' concentration gradients to restore what constantly leaks away through the very channels described above. This pump, embedded in the same membrane described when covering neuron structure, is what keeps the resting potential stable indefinitely rather than gradually fading toward zero, and because it moves unequal numbers of charges each cycle it also makes a small direct contribution to the negative interior voltage.

It helps to picture the resting potential as a charged battery, or water held behind a dam: nothing dramatic is happening moment to moment, but a great deal of stored potential is available the instant a gate opens. That is exactly what happens next. When channels in the membrane open in response to a stimulus, this carefully maintained negative resting charge is disrupted, positive ions rush in, and the voltage begins to shift, the event examined next as depolarization.
